title: Buying or selling a San Diego home with an STRO license: what happens to the license
excerpt: San Diego short-term rental licenses do not transfer when a home sells. What the city's code says, what sellers should do before closing, and how buyers can check a home's license status and plan for their own application.

seo.title: Does a San Diego STRO License Transfer When You Sell?
seo.description: San Diego STRO licenses do not transfer with a sale. What the municipal code says, what sellers and buyers should do, and current Tier 3 and Tier 4 counts.

heroCaption: A licensed short-term rental changes hands on paper at closing. Its STRO license does not.
bodyHtml:
A San Diego home that operates as a licensed short-term rental is often marketed on the strength of its rental income. The license behind that income, however, belongs to a person rather than to the house, and the city's municipal code says plainly that it cannot be transferred. This guide sets out what the rules say as of November 2026, what a seller should do before closing, and what a buyer should verify before counting on short-term rental revenue.

As of November 2026

Rules and figures below come from the San Diego Municipal Code, Chapter 5, Article 10, Division 1 (Short-Term Residential Occupancy), and the City Treasurer's STRO page, which reported license counts as of November 6, 2026. Check both before you act, since counts change weekly.

Does a San Diego STRO license transfer when the home is sold?

No. Section 510.0106(e) of the San Diego Municipal Code states: "Licenses are not transferrable." The City Treasurer's guidance is more specific: STRO licenses "are not transferrable from host to host or property location." When a licensed home sells, the seller's license does not pass to the buyer. A buyer who wants to rent the home short term must apply for a license in their own name, and the city treats that as a new application.

The reason sits in the code's definitions. Section 510.0102 defines a license as one "issued to a host," and a host as "a natural person who has the legal right to occupy the dwelling unit and to allow short-term residential occupancy." The license attaches to that person and that address together. A change in either one ends its usefulness.

Why does this matter more for whole-home rentals?

Whole-home short-term rentals of more than 20 days a year need a Tier 3 license (outside Mission Beach) or a Tier 4 license (in Mission Beach). Both tiers are capped, so a buyer cannot assume a new license will be available. Home-share licenses (Tier 2) and part-year licenses for 20 days or fewer (Tier 1) are not capped.

The Treasurer's counts as of November 6, 2026:

  • Tier 3, whole home outside Mission Beach: capped at 1% of the city's housing units. 4,863 licenses issued, 798 remaining.
  • Tier 4, whole home in Mission Beach: capped at 30% of the Mission Beach planning area's housing units. 1,099 issued, none remaining. The waitlist application period is closed.
  • Tier 1 and Tier 2: no cap. Tier 2 covers home sharing in the host's primary residence only.

For a Tier 3 home, a buyer may be able to obtain a new license while licenses remain under the cap. For a Mission Beach home, the practical answer today is that a buyer cannot expect a whole-home license at closing. Section 510.0106(c) allows Tier 3 and Tier 4 licenses to be issued by lottery when demand exceeds supply, and the city maintains a Tier 4 waitlist; neither guarantees timing. Our STRO license guide tracks the current Tier 3 count from the city's open data.

What should a seller do before closing?

A seller's license ends its usefulness at closing, but the seller still has obligations that run to the end of their ownership. Four steps cover most situations.

1. Decide what happens to future reservations

Because the license cannot move to the buyer, stays booked for dates after closing are not covered by the seller's license. Sellers and buyers should agree in writing, before listing the closing date, whether those reservations will be cancelled and refunded or whether the buyer will have their own license in place first. The city's rules do not address this hand-off, so it belongs in the purchase negotiation. Platforms each have their own cancellation terms and penalties, which a seller should check before accepting a closing date.

2. Cancel the license with the city

The Treasurer's page directs a host who has sold the property to submit the STRO cancellation form to stro@sandiego.gov, and notes that only the host can request the cancellation. Fees are not refunded.

3. Close out transient occupancy tax

Short-term rental operators collect transient occupancy tax (TOT) for the city. The Treasurer's TOT page asks short-term rental operators to notify the office of their intention to cease operations and to review their records to confirm all tax due was reported and remitted. The last return should cover every stay through the final checkout.

4. Take down or update listings

Section 510.0107(l) requires the host's license number and TOT certificate number on all advertisements. Once the seller's license is cancelled, any listing that still shows it is out of compliance, whoever operates it.

What should a buyer check before counting on rental income?

A buyer underwriting a purchase on short-term rental revenue should treat the license as something to be earned, not something being sold. Three checks help.

  • Confirm the current license and tier. The city publishes active licenses, with address, tier and expiration date, on its open data portal. A home listed as "licensed" shows you what tier the seller held, which tells you which pool you would apply to. It does not tell you that you will get a license.
  • Check availability in that tier on the day you write the offer. Tier 3 still had room on November 6, 2026; Tier 4 did not. If the home is in Mission Beach, model the purchase without whole-home short-term income unless and until you hold a license.
  • Check your own eligibility. Section 510.0104(a)(2) states that "a host may only hold one license at a time." A buyer who already holds a license on another home cannot add a second. Section 510.0106(c) also bars applicants with pending enforcement actions or a license revoked within the prior 12 months.

Rental income projections from a seller reflect the seller's license, pricing and management. A buyer who will hold a different tier, or none, should rebuild those numbers. Cardo's free earning estimate starts from the home itself and the license it can realistically hold.

How does a new owner apply?

A new owner applies through the city's STRO portal like any other host. The Treasurer's FAQ notes that an applicant who recently purchased the home will have to attach documentation showing they are the new owner, such as the deed or a change of ownership statement. Only a host, meaning a natural person with the legal right to occupy the unit, may apply (Section 510.0105(a)).

As of the fee schedule effective March 1, 2025, a Tier 3 or Tier 4 license costs $41 to apply and $1,129 for the license, both non-refundable. Licenses in every tier expire two years from issuance, and the city emails renewal notices 60 days before expiration.

Once licensed, a Tier 3 or Tier 4 host takes on the same ongoing duties as any other: a two-night minimum guest stay, use of the license for at least 90 days a year (Section 510.0107(c)), quarterly reporting, a local contact who can respond to complaints within one hour, and the license and TOT numbers on every listing. Our earlier piece on STRO permits, TOT and staying compliant covers those duties in more detail.

Can the home be sold to an LLC or trust and keep the license?

The code does not provide a route for that. A license is issued to a host, who must be a natural person, and it cannot be transferred. Retitling a property does not move a license to a new person. Owners considering an entity transfer, a trust, or a sale to a family member should ask the Treasurer's STRO office and their own attorney how the change affects the license before recording anything.

What about homes outside the City of San Diego?

Everything above applies to the City of San Diego only. Coronado, Del Mar, Encinitas, Carlsbad, Oceanside and unincorporated San Diego County each set their own short-term rental rules, permit types and transfer provisions. A buyer of a North County or Coronado home should read that city's ordinance directly.

The short version

  • San Diego STRO licenses belong to the host and do not transfer with a sale.
  • Sellers should settle future reservations in the purchase agreement, cancel the license, file a final TOT return, and remove the license number from listings.
  • Buyers should check the home's tier and that tier's availability before relying on short-term rental income. As of November 6, 2026, Tier 3 had 798 licenses remaining and Tier 4 (Mission Beach) had none.
  • A new owner applies as a new host with proof of ownership.

Cardo handles STRO applications, renewals, local-contact duties and TOT filings for the homes it manages. Owners buying or selling a licensed home can request an estimate or read how management works on switching managers.

This article is general information as of November 2026, not tax or legal advice. Rules and license counts change; confirm current requirements with the City of San Diego Office of the City Treasurer and a qualified professional before buying, selling or applying.
